routes.description: Defend libertarian agency by separating causal compulsion from non-causal determination, then resist naturalist exhaustion through Bradleyan experiential idealism.
routes.successCriteria: Show that lawful description does not eliminate sourcehood or modal alternatives and that idealism integrates dimensions of experience omitted by reductive naturalism.

motionBridge.description: Libertarian sourcehood and Bradleyan idealism jointly withstand determinist and naturalist pressure better than the pragmatic alternative.

centralBridges.description: Mathematical determination does not itself establish causal compulsion, lack of control, or absence of agential sourcehood.
Scientific and intellectual models do not exhaust felt, moral, aesthetic, volitional, and agential reality.
Bradleyan truth remains constrained by resistant experience, action, coherence, and intellectual satisfaction.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Ordinary practical and moral life supplies defeasible evidence for a real distinction between agency and mere bodily occurrence.

routes.description: Maintain determinist pressure on libertarian alternatives while preserving practically indispensable freedom and a naturalistically restrained account of experience.
routes.successCriteria: Show that the pro account does not secure alternatives under fixed conditions and that pragmatic freedom and experiential modeling meet practical burdens without Bradleyan metaphysics.

motionBridge.description: Compatibilist pragmatism answers the relevant pressures without requiring libertarian branching, irreducible agency, or an existent absolute.

centralBridges.description: Fixed laws and complete states appear to determine a unique future even when determination is described as non-causal.
Freedom remains meaningful through its functions in responsibility, incentives, praise, blame, and behavioral regulation.
Experience can be treated as inquiry's subject matter while physical objects remain useful models without non-natural mental substance.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Changing past facts or laws does not answer a consequence argument that expressly holds those conditions fixed.

sectionJudgments.title: Agency and the Laplacean challenge
sectionJudgments.rationale: This section fixes the initial motion-level conflict between agency as a practical datum and determinism from complete physical information.

proSelections.proposition: Agency is needed to make sense of practical life, while objections to libertarian agency rely on contestable physicalist and closure assumptions.
proSelections.attributionBasis: Folley directly asks Hawkins about his libertarian position, and Hawkins gives an uninterrupted first-person explanation of its practical and metaphysical basis.

response.rationale: As the first selected move chronologically, this is a constructive foundation rather than an answer to an already selected opposing move.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The move clearly establishes an affirmative starting point, though it concedes that compatibilism captures much of the practical datum.

precisionFindings.rationale: The practical need for agency is recoverable and qualified, but the exact additional feature supplied only by libertarianism remains compressed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Hawkins treats agency as strongly supported by practical life while expressly acknowledging that compatibilism explains much of the same material.

charity.alternative: Compatibilism can preserve most of the agency needed for ordinary practical and philosophical life.
charity.decisiveQualification: Hawkins expressly grants that compatibilism supplies most of the practical benefit before claiming that libertarianism preserves something further.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The datum-to-metaphysics inference is intelligible, but the bridge from indispensable practice to specifically libertarian agency remains underdeveloped.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Everyday practical intelligibility is relevant evidence, yet it does not independently discriminate libertarianism from the compatibilism Hawkins partly credits.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the pro motion by supplying the affirmative foundation for preserving consequential agency.

representationalCharity.rationale: Compatibilism is represented as recovering most practical agency rather than dismissed through a weakened reconstruction.

proSelections.evidenceBasis: The bounded excerpt states that practical life requires some notion of agency and explicitly grants that compatibilism provides most of it.

conSelections.proposition: Complete knowledge of particle positions and natural laws would permit derivation of later events and therefore appears to exclude doing otherwise.
conSelections.attributionBasis: Folley explicitly frames the inherited naturalist objection through Laplace's demon and asks Hawkins where its inference against alternatives fails.

components.text: Whether practical agency can survive complete derivability from physical states and laws.

response.rationale: The hypothetical directly tests the pro foundation by asking whether complete lawful derivability rules out the genuine alternatives libertarian agency requires.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It squarely reaches the decisive incompatibility issue, though it presents the derivability premise as an intuition rather than defending it independently.

precisionFindings.rationale: The idealized information, governing laws, predicted outcome, and threatened alternative possibilities are all stated with evaluable scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Folley presents a standard idealized challenge interrogatively and does not claim that the hypothetical has already demonstrated determinism.

charity.alternative: Hawkins denies that physicalism, closure, and bottom-up causation should be assumed as the exhaustive metaphysical picture.
charity.decisiveQualification: The challenge is framed as a request to identify the failure rather than as an assertion that Hawkins simply ignores physical explanation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: If complete physical information and laws uniquely entail every later event, the pressure on genuine alternatives follows coherently.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Laplacean model is a relevant thought experiment, but its completeness and unique-derivation assumptions remain hypothetical and undefended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The question directly attacks the motion-level claim that libertarian alternatives withstand deterministic naturalist pressure.

representationalCharity.rationale: Folley presents the strongest naturalist pressure while leaving Hawkins room to dispute its physicalist and causal assumptions.

conSelections.evidenceBasis: The bounded excerpt specifies exhaustive particle and law knowledge, derivation of subsequent events, and the resulting challenge to doing otherwise.

sectionJudgments.title: Non-causal determination and branching alternatives
sectionJudgments.rationale: This exchange tests whether distinguishing mathematical relations from causation actually preserves the alternatives required by libertarian freedom.

proSelections.proposition: Theoretical physics supplies non-causal mathematical relations, whereas experimental causation is intervention-based and perspectival rather than universal past constraint.
proSelections.attributionBasis: Hawkins answers Folley's causation question by distinguishing theoretical truth-functional relations from experimental interventions in a sustained identified turn.

components.text: Whether mathematical derivability establishes a universal causal order running from past states to later actions.
Whether accepting physical explanation requires treating all scientific determination as causal compulsion.

response.rationale: Hawkins directly attacks the inference from lawful derivability to causal constraint by distinguishing theoretical relations from intervention-based experimental causation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply contacts the central causal bridge, though it does not yet establish that unique non-causal determination leaves genuine alternatives available.

precisionFindings.rationale: Theoretical and experimental sciences are clearly distinguished, and the claim is limited to what mathematical relations establish about causation.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conceptual distinction is well motivated, but the stronger conclusion that causation is fundamentally agent-perspectival requires more defense.

charity.alternative: The naturalist treats laws and complete physical states as describing a universal causal order that constrains later action.
charity.decisiveQualification: Hawkins accepts the correctness of theoretical physics while denying that its mathematical relations are themselves causal.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction blocks an immediate inference from mathematical entailment to causation, although the agency-based account of causation remains partly implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The contrast between equations and interventions supports the distinction, but the broader metaphysical conclusion relies heavily on conceptual interpretation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move materially advances the central pro bridge separating lawful determination from causal compulsion.

representationalCharity.rationale: It preserves the legitimacy of theoretical physics and disputes only the added interpretation that its relations constitute universal causation.

proSelections.evidenceBasis: The source-exact excerpt expressly calls the theoretical relation non-causal and contrasts it with controlled intervention in experimental science.

conSelections.proposition: Even time-symmetric non-causal determination undermines libertarian freedom if fixed states and laws still yield only one future rather than branching alternatives.
conSelections.attributionBasis: Folley grants Hawkins's time-symmetric and non-causal description, then directly asks how a uniquely predictable order preserves the libertarian branching picture.

components.text: Whether removing causal direction changes the unique-outcome problem for libertarian alternative possibilities.

response.rationale: Folley accepts the causal distinction for argument's sake and isolates a surviving problem: unique determination may exclude alternatives without causal pushing.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply explicitly contacts the decisive gap in Hawkins's answer and explains why time symmetry alone does not restore branching possibilities.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conditional scope is clear: fixed states and laws, perfect prediction, and the branching conception of doing otherwise.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Folley presents the inference as how the position seems under the specified model and asks Hawkins to distinguish his view.

charity.alternative: Hawkins maintains that mathematical determination may be time-symmetric and non-causal rather than a past-to-future force.
charity.decisiveQualification: Folley grants that characterization and argues that outcome uniqueness, not causal direction, sustains the challenge.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The response cleanly distinguishes causal direction from modal uniqueness and shows why the former distinction alone is insufficient.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The stipulated fixed-state model supports the conceptual objection, though actual physical uniqueness remains assumed rather than empirically established.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the con motion bridge by preserving determinist pressure after the pro side's principal causal distinction.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply grants the strongest form of Hawkins's time-symmetric account before identifying the remaining modal problem.

conSelections.evidenceBasis: The bounded evidence expressly grants prediction of past and future while arguing that the multiple-branching picture remains undermined under non-causal determinism.

sectionJudgments.title: Pragmatic freedom and metaphysical agency
sectionJudgments.rationale: This section compares Folley's functional compatibilism with Hawkins's claim that the same practices presuppose a genuine metaphysical distinction in agency.

proSelections.proposition: A workable society must preserve the real distinction between intentional action and mere bodily occurrence, so practical indispensability supports metaphysical agency.
proSelections.attributionBasis: Hawkins directly takes up Folley's functional examples and argues in an identified response that denying all free will cannot be lived out socially.

components.text: Whether responsibility practices can operate while remaining neutral about a real distinction between agency and bodily occurrence.

response.rationale: Hawkins accepts the practical argument and contends that its required action-versus-spasm distinction cannot be sustained after eliminating genuine agency.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply contacts the decisive metaphysical issue, but it asserts rather than demonstrates that functional distinctions require libertarian agency.

precisionFindings.rationale: The action-versus-spasm distinction is clear, but the exact metaphysical content of agency and why compatibilism cannot supply it remain implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The practical indispensability of distinguishing conduct is established more strongly than the claim that only libertarian metaphysics can ground it.

charity.alternative: Folley preserves freedom functionally through distinctions needed for incentives, responsibility, praise, and blame even under determinism.
charity.decisiveQualification: Hawkins agrees that those social functions are indispensable but disputes their metaphysical neutrality.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from an indispensable practical distinction to specifically libertarian metaphysical agency leaves a material bridge unresolved.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The action-versus-spasm example is relevant, but no independent reason excludes a compatibilist account of that same distinction.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move supports a necessary subsidiary pro bridge by connecting ordinary practice to the reality of agency.

representationalCharity.rationale: It accurately adopts Folley's practical examples and challenges their interpretation rather than denying their compatibilist function.

proSelections.evidenceBasis: The bounded excerpt argues that a society denying free will would lose the distinction between intentional punching and a muscle spasm.

conSelections.proposition: Even a completely deterministic society needs freedom distinctions because incentives and responsibility must track conduct that social responses can influence.
conSelections.attributionBasis: Folley explicitly presents his own compatibilist thought experiment and explains what free-will practices would remain in a fully deterministic society.

response.rationale: This begins a distinct constructive compatibilist route and does not need to be classified as an answer to an earlier selected pro move.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The thought experiment clearly advances the con burden by identifying a robust practical residue of freedom under determinism.

precisionFindings.rationale: The deterministic stipulation, social setting, functional need, and modest practical conclusion are clearly bounded.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Folley uses a stipulated toy society to argue for pragmatic indispensability without claiming to settle every metaphysical question.

charity.alternative: The strongest incompatibilist view holds that complete determinism removes genuine free will altogether.
charity.decisiveQualification: Folley deliberately grants total determination and asks what socially necessary distinctions would nevertheless remain.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The stipulated society coherently supports the conclusion that practical freedom classifications can survive complete determination.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The social-function thought experiment supplies concrete warrant, though it establishes usefulness more clearly than metaphysical adequacy.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly establishes the motion-level compatibilist-pragmatist route under the strongest determinist stipulation.

representationalCharity.rationale: Folley tests his view against an intentionally severe incompatibilist scenario rather than weakening the determinist premise.

conSelections.evidenceBasis: The excerpt stipulates complete determination and argues that even such a society still requires a system differentiating behavior for practical regulation.

sectionJudgments.title: Bradleyan breadth and naturalized idealism
sectionJudgments.rationale: This section compares Bradley's rejection of scientific exhaustiveness with Folley's naturalistic accommodation of experience as inquiry's primary subject matter.

proSelections.proposition: Bradleyan idealism accepts scientific truths but rejects the additional naturalist premise that scientific explanation exhausts all reality and experience.
proSelections.attributionBasis: Invited to explain Bradley, Hawkins gives a sustained historical and philosophical exposition distinguishing science from an added exclusivity assumption.

response.rationale: The move constructively establishes the pro idealist route; its historical prompt is not an already selected opposing argument requiring response classification.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It clearly identifies the precise naturalist premise rejected while preserving the scientific claims that Bradleyan idealism accepts.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between scientific truths and the added exhaustiveness claim is explicit, stable, and carefully limited.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move makes a conceptual claim about an additional premise and supports it by clearly separating scientific explanation from exclusivity.

charity.alternative: Naturalism accepts scientific explanations and adds that no truths or realities lie beyond their exhaustive reach.
charity.decisiveQualification: Hawkins affirms the truths generated by science and rejects only the further 'nothing else' clause.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between accepting science and rejecting scientistic exhaustiveness is explicit and internally stable.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual separation is well defended, although the positive evidence that omitted experiential domains are irreducibly real comes later.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supplies the pro motion bridge against naturalist pressure while avoiding conflict with science itself.

representationalCharity.rationale: Science is granted its explanatory truths, and criticism is confined to the additional claim of metaphysical exhaustiveness.

proSelections.evidenceBasis: The bounded passage accepts scientific explanations and isolates as an additional assumption the claim that there are no other truths.

conSelections.proposition: Experience may be inquiry's primary subject while physical objects remain constructed models, without positing mysterious mental substance beyond naturalism.
conSelections.attributionBasis: Folley's marked turn states his Humean and Carnapian commitments and contrasts naturalistically acceptable experiential priority with mental-substance idealism.

components.text: Whether honoring experiential priority requires reality beyond naturalistically acceptable models and inquiry.

response.rationale: Folley offers a rival accommodation that accepts experience as the target of understanding while resisting an inference to mysterious mental ontology.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It supplies strong issue-bearing contrary material but does not fully contact Bradley's broader claim about moral, aesthetic, and agential dimensions.

precisionFindings.rationale: The naturalistic proposal is recoverable, though 'mental stuff' and the precise ontological status of constructed physical models remain somewhat informal.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Folley presents a restrained possible reconciliation rather than claiming that phenomenalism conclusively defeats Bradleyan idealism.

charity.alternative: Bradleyan idealism holds that experience outruns thought and that reductive or analytic models fail to encompass reality's full character.
charity.decisiveQualification: Folley accommodates experiential priority and disputes the need to construe it as mysterious non-natural mental substance.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The proposal coherently separates experiential subject matter from a substance claim, though its model-to-reality relation remains compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Humean-Carnapian construction is a plausible rival framework, but the excerpt provides limited argument for its adequacy across all experiential domains.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the con motion bridge by offering a naturalistically acceptable alternative to Bradleyan metaphysics.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply preserves the pro emphasis on experience, but the phrase 'mysterious stuff' risks understating Bradley's more structured position.

conSelections.evidenceBasis: The source-exact evidence contrasts mental-substance language with treating experience as what inquiry explains through constructed physical models.

sectionJudgments.title: Structured experience, truth, and the absolute
sectionJudgments.rationale: The final section tests Bradleyan truth against cognitive-structuring objections and then examines whether completion is real or merely regulative.

proSelections.proposition: Truth reunifies abstract thought with felt reality, and idealism follows because inquiry cannot intelligibly step outside experience to compare thought with independent being.
proSelections.attributionBasis: Hawkins continuously explains Bradley's account of feeling, abstraction, expanded modeling, and the intended reunification constituting complete truth.

response.rationale: No earlier selected con move states the correspondence target in a form this span directly answers, so it is globally classified as constructive.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The move gives a substantive constructive theory of truth, though the transition from experiential access to metaphysical idealism remains compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The relation between feeling and thought is recoverable, but 'reunification' and complete truth require further specification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The account motivates experiential constraint, but the stronger rejection of experience-independent reality is not fully established by epistemic access alone.

charity.alternative: Correspondence truth treats thought or language as answerable to independently constituted facts outside experience.
charity.decisiveQualification: Hawkins allows thought to model what lies beyond immediate feeling while denying an intelligible standpoint wholly outside experience.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The feeling-to-abstraction-to-reunification sequence is intelligible, but the epistemic argument for idealism retains a material bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Phenomenological description supports the model, though it does not alone establish the claimed metaphysical conclusion about independent being.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move centrally advances Bradleyan idealism by explaining truth as integration of thought with experienced reality.

representationalCharity.rationale: The correspondence alternative is recognizable, though its capacity to treat experience as evidence of independent reality receives limited development.

proSelections.evidenceBasis: The bounded excerpt describes thought abstracting from felt experience, modeling beyond finite perspective, and truth as their eventual reunification.

proSelections.proposition: The absolute is more than a completed theory because inquiry's normative orientation toward complete truth recognizes completion as more real than partial understanding.
proSelections.attributionBasis: Hawkins directly answers Folley's Peircean comparison, denies Bradleyan agnosticism, and links intellectual, moral, and aesthetic striving to the absolute.

components.text: Whether completed inquiry is merely a useful regulative endpoint or an actually real completion.
Whether the normative direction of inquiry supplies reason to affirm the reality of its completion.

response.rationale: Hawkins expressly rejects the regulative-only interpretation and offers inquiry's orientation toward completion as the reason for Bradley's stronger realism.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply contacts the decisive ontological question, but its warrant risks moving too quickly from normative aspiration to existence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim about the absolute is recoverable, but 'more real' and the relevant mode of recognition remain only partly specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Normative orientation supports treating completion as an ideal, but it does not by itself necessitate an actually existent absolute.

charity.alternative: The absolute may be a Peircean regulative ideal of completed inquiry without existing as a substantial completed whole.
charity.decisiveQualification: Folley's alternative permits the ideal to guide inquiry while remaining agnostic about attainment or substantial existence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from aiming at completion to recognizing an existent, more-real absolute leaves a major modal and ontological bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The normative structure of inquiry is relevant, but it provides weak support for the stronger claim that its endpoint actually exists.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly defends the motion-level Bradleyan commitment against the strongest selected challenge to the absolute.

representationalCharity.rationale: The regulative alternative is directly recognized and distinguished from Bradley's non-agnostic assertion rather than caricatured.

proSelections.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states that inquiry aims toward completion and infers that this pursuit recognizes the completed whole as more real than partial understanding.

conSelections.proposition: Bradley's unstructured felt given is doubtful because ordinary perception appears categorized from the outset, even at the level of learned edges and objects.
conSelections.attributionBasis: Folley distinguishes mind-framed from mind-controlled reality and then presses a direct phenomenological and neuroscientific-accessibility objection to Hawkins's account.

components.text: Whether subjects encounter a felt reality prior to the distinctions and categories employed by reflective thought.

response.rationale: The objection directly challenges the experiential foundation of Bradleyan truth by questioning whether any accessible perception is genuinely unstructured.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It reaches the decisive premise about precognitive feeling, although the anecdotal neuroscience reference is not developed into independent evidence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The accessibility objection is clear, but 'uncategorized' may range between wholly structureless experience and merely pre-reflective experience.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Folley reports difficulty accessing uncategorized perception and frames the point as a challenge rather than a conclusive disproof.

charity.alternative: Hawkins distinguishes immediate felt encounter from the later abstractions and distinctions of reflective thought.
charity.decisiveQualification: The objection targets conscious accessibility and initial categorization rather than claiming that experience is voluntarily invented.

logicalCoherence.rationale: If perception is structured from its earliest accessible stage, the appeal to an unstructured experiential given requires further explanation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: First-person phenomenology and the learned-edge example are relevant but remain anecdotal and only lightly documented.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly attacks a central pro bridge concerning immediate experience as a foundation deeper than thought.

representationalCharity.rationale: Folley carefully separates unavoidable framing from voluntary control and targets the strongest accessibility issue in Hawkins's account.

conSelections.evidenceBasis: The bounded excerpt reports that perception never appears first uncut and later categorized, adding learned perceptual edges as an illustrative challenge.

conSelections.proposition: Bradley's absolute may be only a Peircean regulative ideal of completed inquiry, leaving its substantial existence and eventual attainment unjustified.
conSelections.attributionBasis: Folley explicitly compares the absolute with Peirce's end of inquiry and asks whether Bradley has grounds for certainty rather than agnosticism.

components.text: Whether an ideal of complete reunification establishes an actually existent absolute rather than an aspirational endpoint.

response.rationale: Folley identifies the gap between describing inquiry's ideal completion and establishing that such a completed absolute substantially exists.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The challenge isolates the decisive ontological burden and offers a clear rival interpretation preserving the normative ideal.

precisionFindings.rationale: The contrast between regulative function, substantial existence, agnosticism, and possible attainment is sharply stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Folley does not deny the absolute outright; he asks whether the evidence warrants more than Peircean agnosticism.

charity.alternative: Bradley treats the absolute as the complete integration of truth, feeling, goodness, beauty, and volition.
charity.decisiveQualification: The objection allows that this completion can guide inquiry while questioning whether guidance establishes existence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The regulative-versus-substantial distinction clearly identifies an evidential gap in the pro account of completion.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Peircean comparison supplies a serious live alternative that explains inquiry's orientation without assuming an existent absolute.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly attacks the pro motion-level metaphysical culmination rather than a peripheral feature of Bradley's system.

representationalCharity.rationale: Folley preserves the absolute's possible regulative role and asks precisely what supports Bradley's stronger ontological confidence.

conSelections.evidenceBasis: The bounded evidence compares the absolute with an end-of-inquiry theory and explicitly contrasts possible attainment with agnosticism about existence.

eligibility.completionCriterion: Sustain determinist pressure while showing that pragmatic compatibilism and naturalized experience satisfy the relevant practical burdens.
